content:
Delhi Police have rescued 164 foreign nationals — 92 Indonesians and 72 Malaysians — from what officers described as a major international "cyber slavery" racket, after raiding a call centre in Noida where the victims were allegedly held captive and forced to run online investment scams targeting people in their home countries.

The raid, carried out on Thursday by the Crime Branch's Inter State Cell at a high-rise office in Sector 136, Noida, exposed a network that police say lured young people to India with promises of well-paid jobs, then seized their passports on arrival, confined them in paying-guest accommodation and put them to work defrauding strangers. One Malaysian national, Tan Guan Wei, 25, was arrested at the scene. Two alleged kingpins — Sunil Kumar and Sushil Kumar Bhati — are absconding, police said.

The operation began with an email. About a week before the raid, a foreign national who had arrived in India a month earlier wrote to the Crime Branch saying that dozens of foreigners were being held captive and forced to commit cyber fraud. The tip-off, later traced to a 42-year-old Malaysian man who had escaped the network and contacted the Malaysian embassy, told police that around 60 to 65 people were being held. When officers entered the premises, they found far more: 164 people, aged between 19 and 25, who had been brought to India over the past four months, according to The Print.

Inside the call centre, police recovered 355 mobile phones, 168 desktop computers, 26 laptops, 53 SIM cards and 174 passports — a haul that, officers said, showed the scale of the operation. The premises were allegedly run under the name of a company called SKV Infratech, and the rescued workers had been given phones, laptops and foreign SIM cards to carry out the fraud.

The victims were not merely operating computers, police said. They were trained to run "pig butchering" scams — a form of fraud in which operators create fictitious female identities and social media profiles, cultivate online relationships with victims over weeks, and then persuade them to invest money in fraudulent trading and investment platforms. The syndicate allegedly used websites and APK-based applications, including platforms named Zenttrix and Quantvoro, promising high returns that never materialised. The targets were primarily people in Malaysia and Indonesia.

Conditions for the workers themselves were grim. According to the Deccan Herald, they were kept in paying-guest accommodation, served substandard food, had their movement restricted and were subjected to physical assault if they refused to work. They followed written scripts to cheat people in their own countries, while the money flowed through Indian handlers and bank accounts that police are now tracing.

Joint Commissioner of Police (Crime) Surender Kumar said the investigation had identified the suspected kingpin as Sunil Kumar, who remains at large, while Sushil Kumar Bhati allegedly managed operations, arranging the accommodation and transport. "Both are absconding, both will be arrested soon," Kumar told reporters. A case has been registered at the Crime Branch police station under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, India's criminal code.

The bust is the latest in a pattern that has alarmed law enforcement across Asia. So-called cyber slavery — trafficking people into scam compounds and forcing them to defraud others online — has grown into a vast criminal industry centred on Southeast Asia, where the United Nations has estimated that hundreds of thousands of people have been trafficked into scam operations. What makes the Delhi case striking is the direction of travel: the victims were brought into India, rather than being lured out of it, suggesting the networks are now operating on both sides of the region's borders.

That reversal matters for how the case is handled next. The rescued nationals are now in the care of the authorities, and the Malaysian and Indonesian embassies are expected to be involved in their repatriation — a process that, in similar cases, has taken weeks while identities and travel documents are verified. Police said they are also examining the financial trail to identify the wider international network, trace the proceeds of crime and establish the role of each suspect.

For the victims, the rescue ends months of captivity, but the questions it raises will linger. How did a network operating openly from a Noida office block recruit 164 people across two countries without detection? How many similar operations are running undetected in other Indian cities? And how many of the people defrauded through Zenttrix, Quantvoro and the other platforms will ever recover their money? Delhi Police say the investigation is continuing, and that more arrests will follow. As [The Print reported](https://theprint.in/india/delhi-police-crime-branch-unit-busts-cyber-slavery-racket-rescues-164-foreign-nationals-from-noida/3110239/), the raid began with a single email from a man who had escaped — and ended with one of the largest cyber slavery rescues India has seen.

The case is a reminder that the online scams flooding phones across Asia are often built on a second crime: the trafficking of the very people forced to make the calls. India has grappled with cybercrime before — the country was recently the target of what Google described as the first fully autonomous AI cyberattack. [Read about that attack here](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/google-first-fully-autonomous-ai-cyberattack-november-2026). But this week's raid in Noida shows the human cost behind the screens: 164 young people who travelled to India for a job, and found themselves prisoners of a fraud machine instead. India and the United States, meanwhile, continue to negotiate on trade as New Delhi faces new tariff pressure from Washington. [Read about the delayed India-US trade deal signing](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/india-us-trade-deal-signing-delayed-november-2026).
summary: Delhi Police have rescued 164 Indonesian and Malaysian nationals from a "cyber slavery" racket in Noida, where victims lured by fake job offers had their passports seized and were forced to run pig-butchering investment scams; one man was arrested and two alleged kingpins are absconding.
title: Delhi Police bust 'cyber slavery' racket in Noida, rescue 164 Indonesians and Malaysians forced to run online scams
